e.etymology: An English form of the Irish name Dubhan, from dubh, 'black, dark', with a diminutive ending, or of the surname O Dubhain, 'descendant of Dubhan'.

assoc.t: Duane Reade, New York City drugstore chain

e.meaning: defender of men (from Alexander or Alexandra)
e.etymology: A pet form of Sandra, Alexandra and Cassandra for girls and, especially in Scotland, of Alexander for boys. It is also the ordinary word for sand-colored hair.
namesakes: Sandy Koufax (Hall of Fame Dodgers pitcher)
Sandy Olsson (Olivia Newton-John's character in Grease)

assoc.t: Hurricane Sandy, which hit New Jersey and New York in 2012
sandy, the ordinary word for sand-covered or sand-colored
Sandy, the dog in Little Orphan Annie
Sandy, Olivia Newton-John's good girl in Grease

e.meaning: from Lassy, a town in Normandy
e.etymology: From the Norman surname de Lacy, brought to England by a family from Lassy in Normandy. Today it is also heard as the word lacy, 'like lace'.

assoc.t: lacy, the ordinary word for made of or like lace

e.etymology: A K spelling of Corey, a surname turned first name whose source is debated; it is often traced to the Old Norse personal name Kori. The K form arose in 20th-century America.
namesakes: Korey Wise (one of the exonerated Central Park Five)

e.etymology: From Hebrew Lemuel, 'devoted to God', the king whose mother's advice fills Proverbs 31. Jonathan Swift gave the name to Lemuel Gulliver.
A Dutch and Spanish form of Adelheid, from Germanic adal, 'noble', and heid, 'kind, sort', which makes it a cousin of Adelaide and Alice.
From an English surname taken from several small places, Old English blaec, 'black, dark', plus leah, 'woodland clearing'.
A modern American name of unclear origin, close in sound to Layla, Kayla and Saylor.
From Old Norse Thyri, the name also written Thyra, borne by a 10th-century queen of Denmark. It is probably a compound containing the name of the god Thor.
From the surname Caine, which has several sources, including the Norman city of Caen and the Irish and Manx name Kane, from cath, 'battle'. It is also read as a spelling of the biblical Cain.

assoc.t: sounds like Cain, who kills his brother Abel in Genesis
Michael Caine, the British actor
The Caine Mutiny, WWII novel and Humphrey Bogart film
Caine, the AI ringmaster of The Amazing Digital Circus

e.note: Sounds identical to Cain, the Bible's first murderer.

e.etymology: A modern American name in the pattern of Kayla and Layla with an initial D.
A respelling of Wesley, an English place name and surname from Old English west plus leah, 'meadow, clearing'. It became a first name in honor of John Wesley, founder of Methodism.

e.meaning: the grain; also short for Ryan
e.etymology: Used as a short form of Ryan and as the English word for the cereal grain, from Old English ryge. Rye is also a surname and a town name in England and New York.

assoc.t: rye, the grain behind rye bread and rye whiskey
The Catcher in the Rye, J. D. Salinger's novel
Rye, New York, a Westchester County suburb

e.etymology: In the US a recent boys' name in the family of Makai, Zakai and Nakai, built around the popular Kai sound. Sakai is also a common Japanese surname and a large city near Osaka.
A German short form of Konrad, from Old High German kuoni, 'bold', and rat, 'counsel'. It came into English use from German in the 20th century.

assoc.t: Kurt Cobain, Nirvana frontman

e.etymology: A Swahili name, the East African form of Arabic Bakr, as in Abu Bakr, the first caliph. American name books often gloss it as 'of noble promise'.
namesakes: Bakari Sellers (CNN commentator and former South Carolina legislator)

e.etymology: A modern elaboration in the family of Mila and Milana, Slavic names built on mil, 'dear, gracious', and close in sound to Emiliana and Liliana. Miliana is also a town in Algeria.
A respelling of Alani, the Hawaiian word for the orange, both the fruit and the tree. The name also echoes lani, 'sky, heaven'.

assoc.t: Alani Nu, energy drink brand (spelled Alani)

e.meaning: resurrection (as a short form of Anastasia)
e.etymology: From an English surname that began as a medieval pet form of Eustace. As a girls' name, popular in the 1970s, it is also explained as a short form of Anastasia, Greek for 'resurrection'.
namesakes: Stacey Abrams (Georgia politician and voting-rights activist)

assoc.t: Stacy's Mom, 2003 Fountains of Wayne hit (spelled Stacy)
Stacy, internet slang for a stereotypically popular woman

e.etymology: The French-style spelling of Edmund, from Old English ead, 'wealth, fortune', and mund, 'protection'. Edmund was a 9th-century king of East Anglia venerated as a saint.
namesakes: Edmond Dantes (hero of The Count of Monte Cristo)

assoc.t: Edmond, Oklahoma, a suburb of Oklahoma City

e.etymology: A spelling of Maite, from the Basque word maite, 'beloved, love'. In Spanish it also serves as a contraction of Maria Teresa.
The Spanish form of Adelaide, from Old High German Adalheid: adal, 'noble', plus heit, 'nature, character'. Alice is a doublet of the same name.
A respelling of Raven, the English word for the large black bird, from Old English hraefn. Raven became a given name in the 20th century.
From Hebrew Aviel, 'God is my father'. In the Old Testament, Abiel is the grandfather of King Saul and also one of David's warriors.

e.meaning: one who lived near a stone cross
e.etymology: From the English word cross and the surname given to someone who lived by a roadside cross or a crossroads. The word goes back to Latin crux.

assoc.t: the cross, central symbol of Christianity
cross, an everyday word for annoyed or angry
Alex Cross, James Patterson's detective
Cross, maker of pens

e.note: Carries a strong Christian reading; cross is also an everyday word for annoyed.

e.etymology: The Spanish diminutive of Juana, the feminine of Juan (John), from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'. It was a top-100 name for American girls in the 1920s and 1930s.
From Latin silvester, 'wooded, of the forest', from silva, 'wood'. Saint Sylvester I was pope in the time of Constantine; his feast falls on December 31.
namesakes: Sylvester Stallone (star of Rocky and Rambo)

assoc.t: Sylvester the Cat of Looney Tunes, Tweety's pursuer
Sylvester Stallone, star of Rocky and Rambo

e.etymology: A modern spelling of Connor, the English form of Irish Conchobhar, usually read as 'lover of hounds'. Conchobar mac Nessa is the king of Ulster in Irish legend.
The Italian form of Paul, from the Roman family name Paulus, 'small, humble'. The apostle Paul made it one of the most widespread Christian names.
namesakes: Paolo Banchero (NBA forward for the Orlando Magic)

e.etymology: A respelling of Malia, the Hawaiian form of Mary, with the -iya ending of Aaliyah. Malia and its spellings jumped in 2009, when Malia Obama moved into the White House.
A respelling of Kyra, from Greek kyria, 'lady', the feminine of kyrios, 'lord'. Kyra is also used as a feminine of Cyrus and as a spelling of Kira.
The Hebrew form of Naphtali, a son of Jacob and founder of one of the twelve tribes of Israel. In Genesis his name is explained by Rachel's words about wrestling with her sister.
namesakes: Naftali Bennett (former prime minister of Israel)
